newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU loses 30 bln Ecus a year in transit fraud.
newsitem.headline: EU loses 30 bln Ecus a year in transit fraud.

text.p: The European Union loses up to 30 billion Ecus in revenue as a result of smuggled goods and forged documents, a leading member of a European Parliament inquiry into transit fraud said on Thursday.
"Fraud concerning goods brought into the market-place in Europe could (be) 30 billion Ecus," said Edward Kellet-Bowman, the author of the committee of inquiry's report.
The inquiry, which started in December 1995, was the first to be launched under new investigative powers granted by the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.
Criminals were making "vast profits" from the EU's archaic paper-based transit system, he told a news conference.
The system allows goods lorries to transit EU member states tax free, only paying customs duties, value-added tax and excise duties at their final destination outside the Union.
But many operators forge their documents and offload cigarettes, alcohol and other high value goods on the EU market. The goods never arrive in the city where the taxes must be paid.

Abuse of the system -- designed in the 1960s for six EU members but now handling 18 million operations a year in the 15 EU states and eight neighbouring countries -- has blown huge holes in the EU budget and national budgets, Kellet-Bowman said.
The black market in cigarettes, which accounts for up to 25 percent of all sales in some member states, was destroying legal traders, the British Conservative Euro-MP added.
His report, which will be available on the Internet, calls for the swift introduction of a computerised transit document system and its extension from road to maritime transport.

John Tomlinson, the chairman of the committee of inquiry, criticised the EU states for their reluctance to replace their fragmented national customs services by a unified system and for failing to recognise computerisation was in their own interest.
"While they are arguing about who pays for it...the citizens of the member states are losing out," he said, adding that the EU was prepared to foot half the 50-million-Ecu computer bill.
Switzerland's lax transit rules were undermining the system still further, British Conservative Tomlinson said.
It was not for nothing that a quarter of all transit lorries passed through Switzerland, even cargoes of American cigarettes arriving in Antwerp and destined for Azerbaijan, he pointed out.
Kellet-Bowman said the member states must step up controls at the EU's external borders -- including coasts and airports -- and that involved training and paying customs officers properly.
"People who are paid (low wages) with these great containers of wealth passing them by are subject to temptation," he said.
